Ports: one per audience ​

Verified against primary documentation and source on 2026-10-12.

What a port separates ​

A port is the finest thing the network can tell apart. Kubernetes NetworkPolicy controls "traffic flow at the IP address or port level (OSI layer 3 or 4)" and has no way to match an HTTP path (Network Policies). Services and load balancer target groups also select ports, not paths. Edge routes do match paths, at layer 7, but only for traffic already admitted to the port they point at, and the pod cannot tell which route a request came through.

So a port is where one audience can be admitted and another refused. Two protocols spoken by the same audience gain nothing from separate ports: every caller allowed on one is allowed on the other, so the network enforces nothing new, and each extra port is one more Service port, route, NetworkPolicy rule, probe and load balancer health check to keep in step.

gRPC is an HTTP/2 path ​

gRPC is defined entirely as HTTP/2 framing. A call is an HTTP/2 request whose path is "/" Service-Name "/" {method name}, whose content-type is application/grpc with an optional suffix such as +proto, and whose result travels in a grpc-status trailer (gRPC over HTTP2).

Connect uses the same procedure paths. "Bidirectional streaming requires HTTP/2, but the other RPC types also support HTTP/1.1"; unary calls use application/proto or application/json, and streaming calls use application/connect+proto or application/connect+json (Connect protocol). "By default, connect-go servers support ingress from all three protocols", meaning Connect, gRPC and gRPC-Web, on the same handler (Getting started).

A server therefore tells requests on one port apart by path and content type:

RequestPathContent typeHTTP
gRPC/acme.billing.v1.Invoices/Getapplication/grpc2
Connect unary/acme.billing.v1.Invoices/Getapplication/proto or json1.1 or 2
gRPC health/grpc.health.v1.Health/Checkapplication/grpc2
Kubernetes httpGet/-/readinessnone1.1
Other routesAnything else, such as /mcpDefined by the route1.1 or 2

Google's own APIs serve gRPC and REST/JSON this way, on one host and port (Google Cloud research).

HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 on one port ​

Over TLS, the client and server agree on the version through ALPN during the handshake. Without TLS, HTTP/2 starts "with prior knowledge" (RFC 9113, section 3.3): the client sends the HTTP/2 preface at once, which an HTTP/1.1 request never starts with, so one listener can accept both.

  • Go: since 1.24, "the server can accept both HTTP/1 and unencrypted HTTP/2 on the same port" when Server.Protocols includes UnencryptedHTTP2. The Upgrade: h2c header is not supported (Go 1.24 release notes). The older golang.org/x/net/http2/h2c NewHandler is deprecated in its favor (h2c).
  • Envoy: an HTTP connection manager with codec_type: AUTO picks the codec per connection and "supports both ALPN for TLS listeners as well as protocol inference for plaintext listeners" (HTTP connection manager). A route can match gRPC alone with grpc: {}, which checks for an application/grpc content type (Route components).
  • Kubernetes: a Service port that speaks prior-knowledge HTTP/2 without TLS declares appProtocol: kubernetes.io/h2c, a standard value since 1.27 (KEP-3726).

Load balancers and proxies ​

Every load balancer below can send gRPC and other routes to one port. They differ in whether one backend definition carries both.

AWS Application Load Balancer ​

No single target group protocol version accepts both HTTP/1.1 clients and gRPC, so the listener forwards to two target groups that point at the same port. A listener rule with a path condition routes "based on the URL in the request" (Condition types for listener rules), so the gRPC service paths go to a gRPC target group and everything else to an HTTP/1.1 one. For the gRPC protocol version, "the only supported listener protocol is HTTPS" and "the only supported action type for listener rules is forward" (Target groups). The full protocol table and health check defaults are in the AWS research.

Google Cloud Application Load Balancer ​

One backend service carries both: HTTP2 for a TLS port, or H2C for a plaintext one, which classic Application Load Balancers do not support. The gRPC backend protocol belongs to Cloud Service Mesh (Google Cloud research).

Gateway API ​

"gRPC traffic can be routed with either HTTPRoute or GRPCRoute", and "for basic gRPC load balancing, GRPCRoute is not technically required because HTTPRoute can do it". GRPCRoute has been in the Standard Channel since v1.1.0. Implementations "may reject" a GRPCRoute whose hostnames overlap an HTTPRoute on the same listener (GRPCRoute), so a port that serves both on one hostname is safest behind a single HTTPRoute with a / prefix, which is what the ADR prescribes for the edge.

Application Gateway for Containers, Azure's Gateway API implementation, configures gRPC only through GRPCRoute, with "no support ... for gRPC in Ingress API" (gRPC with Application Gateway for Containers). There, gRPC on a shared hostname depends on how that implementation treats the overlap.

Istio ​

Istio reads a port's protocol from appProtocol or from a name prefix such as http2- or grpc-, and "if both are defined, appProtocol takes precedence over the port name". Ports named public and private carry no protocol prefix, so without appProtocol Istio tries to detect HTTP and HTTP/2, and "if the protocol cannot automatically be determined, traffic will be treated as plain TCP traffic" (Protocol selection).

Probes on a shared port ​

  • httpGet probes accept a named port, so they can target private or public directly. With scheme: HTTPS "the kubelet sends an HTTPS request skipping the certificate verification" (Probes).
  • grpc probes take a port number only: "you cannot specify the health check port by name". They connect in plaintext unless the GRPCContainerProbeTLS feature gate, alpha and off by default since 1.37, is enabled and mode is set to TLS (Probes; feature gates).

These are why the ADR defaults to httpGet against /-/readiness and /-/liveness on the shared port, and keeps grpc probes for plaintext gRPC-only ports.
